title: Short Stuff: The Dakota
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Dakota, the historic apartment building on Central Park West in Manhattan's Upper West Side. The hosts open with off-topic banter about celebrity sightings, then cover how the building came about: Edward Cabot Clark and architect Henry Janeway Hardenberg built the Van Corlear as a prototype, then the Dakota, which was far up in then-undeveloped territory and was derided as "Clark's folly." They describe its amenities (its own power plant, a boiler system for steam and hot water, a delivery ramp, kitchen balconies, tennis and croquet courts), its early wealthy tenants, its influence on luxury apartment buildings in New York, and famous later residents including Judy Garland, Boris Karloff, and John Lennon and Yoko Ono, who lived there when Lennon was shot outside in 1980. The episode ends with a sign-off and an iHeartRadio production credit.

segments.title: Opening banter and celebrity sightings
segments.summary: Hosts open the short episode and Chuck shares stories about celebrity sightings in New York, including El Fanning, Jessica Chastain, Greta Gerwig and Noah Baumbach, and Tiffany Haddish. Josh steers back to the topic.

segments.title: Introducing the Dakota and its location
segments.summary: The hosts clarify they mean the Manhattan apartment building, not Dakota Fanning. They note it was one of the first apartment buildings in New York and was built on Central Park West when the area was still a dirt road far uptown. Edward Cabot Clark bought the land from an industrialist whose wife did not want to live so far out.

segments.title: Brownstones and the Van Corlear prototype
segments.summary: Before apartments were common, New Yorkers lived in brownstones, and early 1870s apartments were small and dark. Edward Cabot Clark, president of the Singer Sewing Machine company, partnered with architect Henry Janeway Hardenberg to build the Van Corlear, a five-story, 36-unit red brick building on Seventh Avenue that is no longer standing. It improved on earlier buildings with larger rooms, a courtyard, elevators, and a basement delivery ramp.

segments.title: Building the Dakota and an ad-break tease
segments.summary: The Van Corlear rented quickly in 1878, encouraging Clark to buy land from Jacob Henry Schiff farther uptown for the Dakota. The hosts then tease a break and return.

segments.title: Sponsor break and stage break
segments.summary: A short break with a brief remark about Tiffany Haddish and a stage break before the hosts resume the Dakota discussion.

segments.title: Dakota design and amenities
segments.summary: The Dakota improved on the Van Corlear with larger apartments, separated entry areas, and a private power plant from the 1870s. Kitchens had small balconies for disposing of garbage, and the building had a boiler supplying steam and hot water through insulated pipes, plus tennis and croquet courts. Its architectural style is described as a mix of French Renaissance, German Gothic, and Victorian.

segments.title: Clark's folly and early residents
segments.summary: Clark was widely mocked for building so far uptown, and people who rented apartments at the time were mostly widows, widowers, and people waiting to inherit. Clark's gamble paid off. He died before the building was finished. Early tenants were wealthy bankers and business leaders, and the Adams sisters, heirs to a chewing gum fortune, lived there. The hosts also discuss the Tutti Frutti-style tea berry gum flavor.

segments.title: Luxury apartments spread through New York
segments.summary: The Dakota started a trend of luxury apartment buildings with larger rooms and higher ceilings. The Upper West Side and the rest of the city built up more after World War I, and apartments became the norm.

segments.title: Famous later residents
segments.summary: Later residents included Lauren Bacall, Judy Garland, and Boris Karloff. John Lennon and Yoko Ono lived there, and the hosts note Lennon was shot outside the building and that Ono was blamed by some for moving him there.

segments.title: Sign-off and credits
segments.summary: Hosts close the short episode and an iHeartRadio production credit is read.
